title: Twin Lakes Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Twin Lakes well records show a 29 ft median depth. Compare yields, water levels, drilling costs and water-quality checks before buying in Adams County.
h1: What Twin Lakes Well Records Mean for Your Property
intro_html:
A shallow well record does not necessarily describe a household water supply. Around Twin Lakes, 65% of permitted wells are classified for monitoring, while 14% are domestic or household wells. That distinction matters when estimating depth, cost or available water.

Colorado DWR records contain 11,003 permitted wells within 5 miles of Twin Lakes, with 5,371 recorded as constructed. This area includes neighboring Sherrelwood, North Washington, Berkley and Welby. Use the figures below to narrow your research, then check the permit and construction report for the property itself.

sections.heading: Why Twin Lakes Records Skew Toward Shallow Wells
sections.html:
Among the 6,242 records reporting depth, the median is 29 feet, and the middle half falls between 20 and 40 feet. That is a compact range for the recorded population, but the heavy monitoring-well share makes it a poor stand-alone specification for a new household well.

Alluvial and Quaternary Alluvium aquifers appear in the records, alongside many unnamed entries. The cost model assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. A driller needs to identify the intended water-bearing formation rather than price solely from nearby shallow holes. Although 90% of recorded depths are under 100 feet, the deepest record reaches 1,751 feet. Confirm the purpose and aquifer of comparable wells before accepting a depth allowance.

sections.heading: Reported Yield Is Useful, but Household Performance Needs Testing
sections.html:
Only 229 records report a pump yield. Within that subset, the median is 17.0 gpm, with the middle half between 10.0 and 60.0 gpm. Those figures suggest useful production in many tested wells, but they do not establish what an untested Twin Lakes lot will produce.

The low end deserves attention: 5% report less than 1 gpm. For a buyer, that means a favorable neighborhood median cannot replace a sustained pumping test. Ask for the test duration, drawdown and recovery information, along with the installed pump details. A reported yield is neither a guarantee of continuous supply nor permission to pump that amount; allowed use comes from the DWR permit.

sections.heading: Shallow Water Near Twin Lakes Does Not Show a Falling Trend
sections.html:
The 254 records with static water levels show water at a median 10 feet below ground, with the middle half between 7 and 20 feet. Static level is where water stands when the well is not pumping. It is not the total drilled depth or the amount of usable water available under demand.

Decade medians are 24 feet below ground in the 1960s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. These figures do not show a dropping water table; later measurements are shallower. However, they represent different records, not necessarily repeated measurements of the same wells. Have current groundwater conditions checked before planning a basement, excavation or septic system.

sections.heading: A Busy Permit History, Much of It Monitoring Work
sections.html:
Permit activity around Twin Lakes rose from 457 records in the 1980s to 1,947 in the 1990s. The 2010s account for 2,708 permits, compared with 1,034 in the 2020s through the newest recorded permit year, 2025. That recent decade is incomplete, so the totals should not be treated as a straightforward slowdown.

The most active listed entry is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 3,712 records; its label should not be mistaken for a conventional drilling-company name. Named drillers include Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.), with 202, and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.), with 161. Given the monitoring-heavy use mix, this history is not a count of new residential water supplies.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Twin Lakes Well Beyond the Drilled Hole
sections.html:
The supplied model uses $50–$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the recorded median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,400–$2,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,400–$14,000.

Treat those amounts as an initial comparison, not a property-specific quote. The 29-foot median comes from a population dominated by monitoring wells, and your permitted household supply may require a different depth and design. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment and site connections in the proposal. Also clarify how unexpected depth, difficult access and any needed water treatment would be handled before work starts.

sections.heading: Water Quality and Shallow Groundwater Need Separate Checks
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapping identifies 690 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 184 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These are reasons to investigate, not proof that a particular Twin Lakes well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location does not by itself establish contamination at that location or on your parcel.

Review nearby site records and arrange laboratory testing appropriate to the property's surroundings, including discussion of PFAS, bacteria and nitrate testing. Inspect casing, the well cap and surface drainage as well. A shallow water level can complicate septic siting and excavation, while a shallow drilled depth does not guarantee adequate yield. Confirm the wastewater arrangement and coordinate well protection, septic suitability and building plans before committing to the layout.

sections.heading: Before Buying a Lot Between Sherrelwood and Welby
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, not the regional median. Confirm that the authorized uses match your plans for the home, landscaping and any animals. Do not assume a monitoring permit or an existing hole can be used as a household supply. New withdrawals may require augmentation where applicable; resolve the water-supply pathway before designing the house.

Then compare nearby wells in Sherrelwood, North Washington or Welby by use, aquifer, construction and tested yield—not proximity alone. For an existing well, obtain construction records, a current pumping evaluation and laboratory results. For a vacant lot, have drilling access, utility routing, wastewater service and the building footprint reviewed together so the water plan actually fits the site.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Twin Lakes, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Twin Lakes, the median reported depth is 29 feet, and the middle half is 20–40 feet. However, 65% of permits are for monitoring use. Those shallow records should not set the drilling depth for a household supply. Compare wells with the same intended use and aquifer before requesting a bid.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Twin Lakes?
faq.a: The model estimates $50–$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 29-foot median depth, the hole alone is about $1,400–$2,000, while a finished well is about $7,400–$14,000. Because monitoring wells dominate the records, a household well may need a different depth. Get a site-specific proposal covering equipment and connections.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Twin Lakes?
faq.a: The 229 records reporting pump yield have a median of 17.0 gpm and a middle-half range of 10.0–60.0 gpm. However, 5% report less than 1 gpm. Before buying, get a sustained pumping test and review drawdown and recovery. The reported pumping rate does not establish either reliable long-term output or the uses legally allowed by the permit.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Twin Lakes, Colorado?
faq.a: The regional records cannot establish whether an individual well is safe. Mapping shows 690 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 184 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not prove contamination. Review nearby environmental records, inspect the well's sanitary condition and use laboratory testing selected for the property, including discussion of PFAS, bacteria and nitrates.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Twin Lakes?
faq.a: The supplied decade medians do not show a decline: static water was 24 feet below ground in the 1960s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 8 feet in the 2020s. Later readings are shallower. However, these are not necessarily measurements from the same wells, so they cannot establish a property-specific trend. Obtain a current measurement and pumping evaluation.
